items.stem: What is the difference between authentication and authorization?

options.text: Authentication proves who you are; authorization decides what you may do
options.rationale: Correct: authentication establishes identity, authorization grants permissions.

options.text: They are two names for the same check
options.rationale: They are distinct steps with different purposes.
You must establish identity before deciding permissions.
Authentication applies to users and machines alike.

items.explanation: Correct: authentication establishes identity, authorization grants permissions.

items.stem: Which are core Zero Trust principles? (Select TWO)

options.text: Never trust, always verify every request
options.rationale: Correct: Zero Trust verifies each request regardless of origin.

options.text: Enforce least privilege and assume breach
options.rationale: Correct: minimal access and an assume-breach posture are central to Zero Trust.

options.text: Trust any device once it is inside the network perimeter
options.rationale: Implicit perimeter trust is exactly what Zero Trust rejects.

options.text: Grant permanent administrator rights to reduce friction
options.rationale: Standing broad privilege violates least privilege.

items.explanation: Correct: Zero Trust verifies each request regardless of origin.; Correct: minimal access and an assume-breach posture are central to Zero Trust.

items.stem: Which combination counts as genuine multi-factor authentication?

options.text: A password plus a one-time code from a hardware or app authenticator
options.rationale: Correct: this combines something you know with something you have.
Both are the same factor type (something you know).
A username is an identifier, not a factor.
Both are knowledge factors, so this is single-factor.

items.explanation: Correct: this combines something you know with something you have.
